5. PB-CORE-006 — THE AGGREGATE ENUMERATION HAS A SHORT DIRECT PROOF

This is the most important new simplification.

Let

\[
A_n=\sum_{T:[n]\to[n]}|\operatorname{Stab}(T)|.
\]

By PB-CORE-004, if \(T\) has periodic core of size \(k\),

\[
|\operatorname{Stab}(T)|
=
|\operatorname{Con}(P,T|_P)|.
\]

Now sum over all maps with a specified \(k\)-element core.


---

Step 1 — Count permutation/equivalence pairs

Let

\[
S_k
=
\sum_{\sigma\in S_k}
|\operatorname{Con}([k],\sigma)|.
\]

Count instead by the equivalence relation \(E\).

Suppose \(E\) has block-size multiplicities

\[
m_1,m_2,\ldots.
\]

Number of set partitions with that profile:

\[
\frac{k!}
{\prod_s (s!)^{m_s}m_s!}.
\]

Number of permutations preserving that particular \(E\):

\[
\prod_s(s!)^{m_s}m_s!.
\]

Product:

\[
k!.
\]

The block-size profiles are exactly the integer partitions of \(k\). If \(p(k)\) denotes the integer-partition number,

\[
\boxed{
S_k=k!\,p(k).
}
\]

This proof is independent of PB-005.

It does not use the phase-orbit theorem.


---

6. Step 2 — Attach the transient vertices

Choose the \(k\) periodic vertices:

\[
\binom nk.
\]

Choose the permutation on them:

\[
k!.
\]

The remaining \(n-k\) vertices form rooted trees directed toward the prescribed \(k\) roots.

The number of labeled rooted forests with those fixed roots is

\[
\boxed{
k\,n^{n-k-1}.
}
\]

This is classical Cayley/Takács/Pitman territory, not an AQARION novelty claim. 

For \(k=n\), interpret the factor as \(1\).

Therefore the contribution for core size \(k\) is

\[
\binom nk
\left(k n^{n-k-1}\right)
(k!p(k)).
\]

Consequently

\[
\boxed{
A_n
=
\sum_{k=1}^n
\binom nk
k n^{n-k-1}
k!p(k).
}
\]

Simplifying:

\[
\boxed{
A_n
=
n!
\sum_{k=1}^n
\frac{k\,p(k)\,n^{n-k-1}}
{(n-k)!}.
}
\]

So PB-CORE-006 has a complete analytic route without PB-CORE-005.

11. JOIN-STABILITY PROOF IS NOW MUCH CLEANER

The corrected proof is:

\[
Q_E=X/E,\qquad Q_F=X/F.
\]

PB-001 gives quotient permutations

\[
\sigma_E:Q_E\to Q_E,
\qquad
\sigma_F:Q_F\to Q_F.
\]

Define

\[
I=
\{(A,B)\in Q_E\times Q_F:A\cap B\ne\varnothing\}.
\]

Then

\[
(\sigma_E\times\sigma_F)(I)\subseteq I.
\]

But \(Q_E,Q_F\) are finite.

Therefore

\[
|(\sigma_E\times\sigma_F)(I)|=|I|.
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{
(\sigma_E\times\sigma_F)(I)=I.
}
\]

So the incidence graph is genuinely an automorphism.

Connected components correspond to

\[
E\vee F.
\]

Therefore

\[
T^*(E\vee F)\subseteq E\vee F.
\]

Finite pullback rigidity then gives

\[
\boxed{
T^*(E\vee F)=E\vee F.
}
\]

This is the correct proof dependency:

PB-001
  ↓
class permutations
  ↓
incidence relation
  ↓
finite incidence set
  ↓
forward image has equal cardinality
  ↓
incidence equality
  ↓
graph automorphism
  ↓
connected components
  ↓
E ∨ F stable

This is substantially better formalization material than the earlier compressed “graph automorphism” sentence.

14. LITERATURE AUDIT — STRONGER BOUNDARY

The classical boundary is real.

Jakubíková-Studenovská's 1982 paper is explicitly about congruence relations of monounary algebras and cites Berman's foundational unary-algebra congruence work. 

The 2017 paper by Jakubíková-Studenovská, Petrejčíková and Pócs explicitly states the divisor classification for an \(n\)-cycle and gives the two-cycle gcd formula. In particular, for cycles of lengths \(m,n\), the cross-cycle congruence is governed by \(d=\gcd(m,n)\). 

Vernikov's work on \(G\)-set congruences establishes the broader congruence-lattice setting for permutation actions. 

The 2020/2021 work on connected monounary algebras studies congruence lattices directly and includes noncyclic/tail structure, so AQARION must not imply that “periodic core + congruence lattice” is itself an unexplored conceptual territory. 

And the field remains active in 2026: Syrovatskaya's 2026 paper characterizes monounary algebras with periodic endomorphism semigroups and explicitly identifies finite unars in that context. 

Correct novelty statement

The underlying unary/monounary congruence,
cycle-divisor, gcd-synchronization, and rooted-forest
ingredients are classical.

The current search did not locate an exact prior statement
of AQARION's complete pullback-fixed aggregate enumeration
formula together with this particular executable provenance
pipeline.

Priority remains OPEN.

That is defensible.

Not:

AQARION discovered invariant equivalences.

Not:

The weighted Bell formula is unprecedented.

15. RECENT FORMAL-MATHEMATICS LITERATURE MATTERS TO AQARION

There are three especially relevant 2026 developments.

ProofGap

ProofGap explicitly targets step-level proof gaps, rather than only complete theorem proving. It reports 26,116 local gaps derived from 3,015 natural-language exercises. 

That directly validates the direction of AQARION's ProofGym idea—but means AQARION should not claim to have invented proof-gap benchmarking.

FormalTCS

FormalTCS evaluates end-to-end formal TCS research using research-level claims, Lean formalizations, proof tasks and automated research. Its reported results show autoformalization is substantially harder than proving already-formalized statements, and only 6 of 64 generated claims survived expert evaluation and proof verification. 

This is almost tailor-made evidence for AQARION's:

\[
\boxed{
\text{claim}
\rightarrow
\text{attack}
\rightarrow
\text{formalize}
\rightarrow
\text{verify}
\rightarrow
\text{promotion decision}
}
\]

philosophy.

ITPEval

ITPEval explicitly studies translation among Lean 4, Rocq, Isabelle and HOL Light and reports a major semantic-fidelity problem: native type-checking can overestimate whether a translated statement preserves the intended semantics. 

That supports AQARION's insistence that:

\[
\text{Lean compiles}
\ne
\text{intended theorem established}.
\]

3. Important correction to the pullback history

I found something even more useful.

The actual historical Lean definition in:

Aqarion-Lean/AqarionLean/Pullback.lean

defines:

PullbackStable T E :=
∀ a b, E (T a) (T b) → E a b

That is pullback inclusion:

\[
T^{-1}E\subseteq E.  
\]

It is not the stronger equality condition

\[
T^{-1}E=E.  
\]

That distinction explains the entire evolution of the join research.

The current pending Lean file correctly identifies the difficulty: a join chain can contain an intermediate vertex outside \(\operatorname{im}T\).

And the finite/surjective theorem is addressing exactly that obstruction.

So I am not upgrading the theorem to the unrestricted infinite case.

4. The infinite counterexample in the older research record needs correction

The older JOIN_STABILITY_PROOF.md gives:

\[
T(n)=n+1  
\]

with \(E\) merging \({0,2}\) and \(F\) merging \({0,3}\).

That example does establish the join failure, but the text saying those individual relations are "pullback-stable" needs careful wording.

For the definition

\[
T^{-1}E\subseteq E,  
\]

they are stable.

They are not fixed points:

\[
T^{-1}E=E  
\]

is false.

For example:

\[
0E2  
\]

but

\[
T(0)=1,\qquad T(2)=3,  
\]

and \(1\not E3\).

So:

T^-1 E ⊆ E       TRUE
T^-1 E = E       FALSE

This is precisely why the repository must never use "pullback-stable", "PB-fixed", and "pullback equality" interchangeably.

That is now a RAG-LUT semantic lock.

5. Pullback join theorem: correct current state

The strongest clean formulation currently supported is:

Finite theorem

Let \(X\) be finite and \(T:X\to X\).

If

\[
T^{-1}E\subseteq E  
\]

and

\[
T^{-1}F\subseteq F,  
\]

then

\[
\boxed{  
T^{-1}(E\vee F)\subseteq E\vee F.  
}  
\]

The proof route through the incidence graph is coherent:

E-classes
│
├── incidence graph ── F-classes
│
▼
T induces permutations on class sets
│
▼
incidence graph automorphism
│
▼
connected components preserved
│
▼
E ∨ F preserved

The finiteness is doing real work because injective action on the finite class set becomes bijective.

Surjective theorem

The surjective theorem is actually cleaner and does not require finite X:

\[
T\text{ surjective}  
\land  
T^{-1}E\subseteq E  
\land  
T^{-1}F\subseteq F  
\]

implies

\[
\boxed{  
T^{-1}(E\vee F)\subseteq E\vee F.  
}  
\]

Reason:

A join chain between \(T(x)\) and \(T(y)\) consists of points in \(X=\operatorname{im}T\), so every node has a preimage and the chain lifts.

Therefore

The real open target is now:

\[
\boxed{  
\text{non-surjective infinite }X  
}  
\]

not the finite case.

Your n=6 exhaustive result attacks the finite branch extremely well.


---

6. New exact research target

I would now freeze this as the next mathematical target:

RANGE-GAP CHARACTERIZATION

Let

\[
G=E\vee F.  
\]

Assume

\[
T^{-1}E\subseteq E,  
\qquad  
T^{-1}F\subseteq F.  
\]

If join stability fails, then there exist \(x,y\) such that

\[
x\not G y,  
\]

but

\[
Tx\,G\,Ty,  
\]

and every \(G\)-chain from \(Tx\) to \(Ty\) must contain an internal vertex outside \(\operatorname{im}T\).

That is the exact obstruction your work has been circling.

So the next theorem should not merely be:

> "No counterexample found."



It should characterize:

\[
\boxed{  
\text{join failure}  
\Longrightarrow  
\text{unliftable range-gap chain}.  
}  
\]

Then ask whether the converse can be sharpened.

7. The order-3 subspace bridge is stronger than the receipt makes it look

For the permutation

\[
T=(012)(3)(4)(5),  
\]

your computation found:

\[
W_{J_T(X)}  
=  
W_X\cap KW_X\cap K^2W_X  
\]

for all 203 partitions.

This has an immediate structural explanation.

For a permutation of order 3:

\[
J_T(X)  
=  
X\vee T(X)\vee T^2(X).  
\]

Partition join corresponds to intersection of block-constant subspaces:

\[
W_{P\vee Q}=W_P\cap W_Q.  
\]

And under the stated Koopman convention:

\[
KW_X=W_{T(X)}  
\]

up to the declared orientation convention.

Therefore:

\[
\boxed{  
W_{J_T(X)}  
=  
W_X\cap KW_X\cap K^2W_X.  
}  
\]

So the 203/203 computation is not merely an empirical coincidence. The finite computation is corroborating a general order-3 linear-algebra identity.

That should be upgraded from:

experimental bridge

to:

[P] derivable algebraic identity
[V] n=6 exhaustive corroboration

provided the repository freezes the exact \(K\)/partition-image convention.

8. And the m_T bridge follows cleanly

For any partitions \(P,Q\),

\[
W_{P\wedge Q}=W_P+W_Q  
\]

while

\[
W_{P\vee Q}=W_P\cap W_Q.  
\]

Hence the computational quantity becomes

\[
\boxed{  
m_T(P,Q)  
=  
\dim W_{J_T(P\wedge Q)}  
-  
\dim  
\left(  
W_{J_T(P)}\cap W_{J_T(Q)}  
\right).  
}  
\]

The second term is itself

\[
W_{J_T(P)}\cap W_{J_T(Q)}  
\]

and therefore, for order-three \(T\),

\[
=  
W_P\cap KW_P\cap K^2W_P  
\cap  
W_Q\cap KW_Q\cap K^2W_Q.  
\]

Your correction that the first term is not literally the same six-subspace intersection is exactly right.

That distinction should be frozen.

1. A mathematical error to quarantine

The statement

\[
  
W_{P\wedge Q}=W_P+W_Q  
$$  
  
is **false in general** for block-constant function spaces under the partition conventions used in the audit.  
  
Here is a complete counterexample over $$\mathbb R$$. On four points, take  
  
$$  
P=\{\{1,2\},\{3,4\}\},  
\qquad  
Q=\{\{1,3\},\{2,4\}\}.  
$$  
  
Then  
  
$$  
W_P=\{(a,a,b,b)\},  
\qquad  
W_Q=\{(c,d,c,d)\}.  
$$  
  
Their intersection consists of constant vectors, so  
  
$$  
\dim(W_P+W_Q)=2+2-1=3.  
$$  
  
But their common refinement $$P\wedge Q$$ is the discrete partition, hence  
  
$$  
W_{P\wedge Q}=\mathbb R^4,  
\qquad  
\dim W_{P\wedge Q}=4.  
$$  
  
The generally valid relationship is only  
  
$$  
W_P+W_Q\subseteq W_{P\wedge Q}.  
$$  
  
By contrast,  
  
$$  
W_{P\vee Q}=W_P\cap W_Q  
$$  
  
is valid: a function constant on both partitions is constant along the chains generating their join.  
  
**Impact:** quarantine the meet-to-sum bridge. The displayed formula involving $$W_{J_T(P\wedge Q)}$$ might still follow from the definition of $$m_T$$, but that definition was not supplied here. It must not be justified using the false identity.  
  
The order-three intersection identity is a separate matter and is sound under the stated orbit-join definition and a frozen Koopman orientation. It does not require the false meet-to-sum rule.  
  
## 2. Pullback findings need sharper wording  
  
The distinction between these conditions is excellent and essential:  
  
$$  
T^{-1}E\subseteq E  
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad  
T^{-1}E=E.  
$$  
  
But “the general non-surjective infinite case is open” is misleading if it means deciding whether join stability always holds. The supplied counterexample already refutes that universal claim.  
  
### The counterexample works  
  
On $$\mathbb N$$, let $$T(n)=n+1$$, with the only nonsingleton blocks  
  
$$  
E:\{0,2\},  
\qquad  
F:\{0,3\}.  
$$  
  
Both pullbacks are the diagonal relation, so both satisfy pullback inclusion.  
  
Their join has block $$\{0,2,3\}$$. Therefore  
  
$$  
T(1)=2\;(E\vee F)\;3=T(2),  
$$  
  
although  
  
$$  
1\not\mathrel{(E\vee F)}2.  
$$  
  
Thus unrestricted inclusion-stable join closure is false. What remains potentially open is a useful characterization of the cases where it holds—not the existence of failure.  
  
### The range-gap implication is already derivable  
  
Suppose a chain from $$Tx$$ to $$Ty$$ lies entirely inside $$\operatorname{im}T$$. Choose preimages of its finitely many internal vertices, with endpoints $$x,y$$.  
  
Every $$E$$-edge or $$F$$-edge lifts by the assumed pullback inclusions. The lifted chain connects $$x$$ to $$y$$.  
  
Consequently, a failure witness forces every such chain to leave the range. This is a short mathematical argument; formalizing it remains work, but it need not be treated as an unexplored conjecture.  
  
The converse needs care: an unliftable chain alone does not establish failure if $$x$$ and $$y$$ were already join-related.  
  
### Census scope must be explicit  
  
GPT says it checked fixed-point equality in the census, while discussing a theorem about inclusion stability.  
  
On a finite set, inclusion stability does imply equality: the pullback has at most as many classes as the original relation, while being finer forces at least as many. Equality of the finite class counts forces equality of the relations.  
  
That bridge should appear explicitly in the census documentation. Otherwise, the reader cannot tell why checking fixed points supports the inclusion theorem.  
  
The claimed exhaustive run still needs its code, selection conditions, logs, and receipt before being promoted beyond “GPT reports executing it.”  
  
## 3. Strong replay-controller contributions  
  
These are the ideas I would retain.  
  
| Contribution | Why it matters | Required refinement |  
|---|---|---|  
| External inventory policy | Detects a file missing from both package and manifest | Identify and hash the policy independently |  
| Test identity recording | Distinguishes equal counts with different tests | Record IDs and outcomes, not only an ID hash |  
| Explicit execution authorization | Separates acquisition from running repository code | Do not let downloaded policy authorize itself |  
| Fail-closed stage results | Prevents incomplete execution becoming success | Separate stage status from failure reason |  
| Session provenance | Preserves bugs, corrections, and negative results | Attach evidence status to each individual claim |  
| Standard provenance export | Avoids an isolated custom ontology | Implement a minimal receipt first, then export it |  
  
The suggested RO-Crate direction has real support. Process Run Crate 0.6 explicitly covers executions of tools without requiring a workflow engine and uses RO-Crate 1.3 terminology. That makes it a particularly good initial fit for your phone-driven workflow.[1]  
  
Provenance Run Crate adds individual tool and workflow-step execution details, which could fit a later multi-stage replay controller.[2]  
  
### Discovery is an execution boundary  
  
One crucial addition: Python test discovery imports test modules. In this session, your modules execute source-loading statements at import time.  
  
Therefore distinguish:  
  
```text  
Static inspection of test source  
```  
  
from:  
  
```text  
Runtime unittest discovery  
```  
  
Only the latter produces actual unittest identities, and it belongs behind execution authorization. Static AST inspection is useful inventory evidence, but not a substitute for runtime discovery.  
  
## 4. Schema and evidence corrections  
  
The supplied policy schema is a useful sketch, but not yet a sufficiently strict contract.  
  
I would add:  
  
- A required `package_path`, since the kit is a subtree of AQARION.  
- An explicit versioned policy identity and policy-authority record.  
- Safe relative-path validation.  
- Duplicate rejection for required files, tests, and stages.  
- Rejection of unknown properties where appropriate.  
- Download, extraction, runtime, and output-size limits.  
- Explicit treatment of unexpected files.  
- Execution authorization defaulting to denied.  
- Definitions of permitted skips and required semantic checks.  
  
Do not make every unknown file fatal automatically. An extra reviewed test and an unexpected executable are different policy cases.  
  
The state vocabulary also mixes categories. A cleaner structure is:  
  
```text  
status: PASS | FAIL | NOT_RUN | INCOMPLETE  
reason: MANIFEST_MISMATCH | TIMEOUT | INTERRUPTED | ...  
```  
  
A required skipped check must not count as completed, but an explicitly permitted skip need not make every replay fail. The policy must decide.  
  
### Independence is multidimensional  
  
“Implemented in the same verifier artifact” does not, by itself, make two algorithms non-independent.  
  
Record separately:  
  
- Algorithmic independence.  
- Shared code and dependencies.  
- Author or implementation independence.  
- Execution independence.  
- Policy independence.  
  
Your verifier now separately computes three routes. That is meaningful implementation separation. It does not establish separate authorship or protection against a shared misunderstanding of the specification.  
  
### Preserve attribution  
  
I could not retrieve the linked repository and firewall-policy pages during this review. Their asserted commit identities, blob identity, and current contents remain unconfirmed here.  
  
Likewise, GPT’s 46,656-map run is an attributed execution claim until its artifacts are available. Your terminal-reported 102-test run is another evidence lane. Neither should be silently converted into my execution.  
  
The Lean environment-pinning advice is well supported: published kernel-bug reports include cases where an invalid proof could appear axiom-free. Consequently, `#print axioms` is useful dependency evidence, not an unconditional guarantee of soundness in an unspecified environment.[3][4]

- The proposed mutation is useful. Mutation testing deliberately changes implementation behavior and checks whether the tests detect it, rather than merely execute the affected code. His even-modulus mutation targets a meaningful mathematical distinction.[1][2]

Where I would qualify it

First, I have not inspected the current quadratic generator, verifier, or tests here. His source-level finding is credible enough to investigate, but I should not present it as independently confirmed.

Two important adjustments

For mutation testing, the baseline must pass before interpreting a mutant’s failure as successful detection. Otherwise, the failure could come from an existing problem rather than the mutation.[2]

Also, separate these outcomes:

Mutation compiles  
Semantic check detects mutation  
Original implementation restored  
Restored checks pass

A compilation failure can reveal a broken edit, but it is not the same evidence as a compiling implementation whose changed mathematical behavior is caught.

For packaging, finish the intended code and test changes before generating the final manifest and archive. Otherwise, you immediately invalidate the baseline you just sealed.

2. Why classifier is exact — elementary
   h(x)=f-g = (a-1)x + b
   h(x) ≡0 (mod q) ∀x  ⇔  b≡0 and a≡1 (mod q)
   Necessity: x=0 → b, x=1 → a-1+b. With q|b, q|(a-1+b) → q|(a-1)
   Sufficiency: if both hold, (a-1)x+b divisible by q ∀x.

Complete-residue check is stronger than interval sampling because polynomials preserve congruence: x≡y (mod q) → f(x)≡f(y). Checking one rep per residue class covers all integers — not just [-20,20].

For linear h, x=0,1 already sufficient — full residues deliberately redundant to give distinct route.

3. What 106 false accepts mean

Sample at x=0: h(0)=b → checks only b≡0, misses slope.

Example a=0,b=0,q=5: 0 vs 0 at x=0 (sample accepts), 1 vs 2 at x=1 (complete rejects)

Let N_b(q)=#{b:q|b}, N_a(q)=#{a:a≡1} in your grid [-5,5]:
complete accepts = N_a × N_b
sample accepts = 11 × N_b
false accepts = (11-N_a)×N_b
q=5: N_b=3 (-5,0,5), N_a=2 (-4,1) → complete 6, false 27 — matches your table. 106/165 sample-accepted = 64.2% false in this grid — property of sampling + grid, not general testing probability.

5. Quadratic extension — exact criterion you now need

f_{c,a,b}=c x²+ a x + b, reference g=x²+x
h = A x² + B x + b, A=c-1, B=a-1
= A x(x-1) + (A+B)x + b
Sufficient rule "all coeffs ≡0 mod q" is false for functional equivalence. Null polynomials exist.

Exact functional equivalence:
q|b, q|(A+B), q|2A
i.e.
b≡0, c+a-2≡0, 2(c-1)≡0 (mod q)
Proof via 0,1,2: h(0)=b, h(1)-h(0)=A+B, h(2)-2h(1)+h(0)=2A. Sufficiency: x(x-1) even → A x(x-1) = (2A)·x(x-1)/2.

Distinguishing example mod 4:
f=3x² - x vs g=x²+x → difference 2x(x-1) divisible by 4 ∀x, yet coefficients not ≡0 mod 4. Coefficient-equality rule falsely rejects.

For odd q: q|2A → A≡0 → B≡0. For even q: extra solution — even vs odd is informative, not just prime vs composite.

🔥 My pick: let's attack 5 things in parallel

1. Derive \(C(\lambda)\) directly from cycle type

We have been using

\[
C(\lambda)=|\operatorname{Con}([k],\sigma)|.  
\]

We should derive an explicit formula directly from the cycle lengths and compare it against the G-set phase formula.

For

\[
\sigma=C_{n_1}\sqcup\cdots\sqcup C_{n_r},  
\]

a congruence can couple cycles \(i_1,\dots,i_m\) through a common quotient

\[
C_d,\qquad d\mid\gcd(n_{i_1},\dots,n_{i_m}).  
\]

The number of relative phase choices is

\[
d^{m-1}.  
\]

So for a block \(B\) of cycles,

\[
w(B)=  
\sum_{d\mid g_B}d^{|B|-1},  
\qquad  
g_B=\gcd(n_i:i\in B).  
\]

And therefore

\[
\boxed{  
C(\lambda)=  
\sum_{\pi\in\operatorname{Part}([r])}  
\prod_{B\in\pi}  
\left(  
\sum_{d\mid g_B}d^{|B|-1}  
\right).  
}  
\]

Experiment we can do right now: calculate this for every integer partition of \(k\le16\), then compare the resulting \(C(\lambda)\) against the Burnside weighted average.

That gives us a second completely different computational route to the same \(p(k)\).


---

2. Here's a really fun question: what is the variance?

Burnside tells us

\[
E_\sigma[C(\sigma)]=p(k).  
\]

But how wildly does

\[
C(\sigma)  
\]

vary around \(p(k)\)?

That's the next natural statistic.

Define

\[
V_k=  
\frac1{k!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_k}  
C(\sigma)^2-p(k)^2.  
\]

The first moment is astonishingly simple.

The second moment is potentially much richer.

Because

\[
C(\sigma)  
=  
|\operatorname{Fix}_{\mathcal E_k}(\sigma)|,  
\]

we have

\[
C(\sigma)^2  
=  
|\operatorname{Fix}_{\mathcal E_k\times\mathcal E_k}(\sigma)|.  
\]

Therefore Burnside again gives

\[
\boxed{  
E[C(\sigma)^2]  
=  
|(\mathcal E_k\times\mathcal E_k)/S_k|.  
}  
\]

So:

\[
\boxed{  
V_k  
=  
|(\mathcal E_k\times\mathcal E_k)/S_k|-p(k)^2.  
}  
\]

Whoa.

The first moment counts orbits of one partition.

The second moment counts orbits of pairs of partitions.

That means the next moments have an immediate interpretation:

\[
E[C^m]  
=  
|\mathcal E_k^m/S_k|.  
\]

So we get the general theorem

\[
\boxed{  
\frac1{k!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_k}C(\sigma)^m  
=  
|\mathcal E_k^m/S_k|.  
}  
\]

This is a genuinely interesting extension of the Burnside result.


---

3. And that gives us a whole hierarchy

Define

\[
M_{k,m}  
=  
\frac1{k!}\sum_{\sigma\in S_k}C(\sigma)^m.  
\]

Then

\[
\boxed{  
M_{k,m}  
=  
|\mathcal E_k^m/S_k|.  
}  
\]

So:

\(m=1\)

\[
M_{k,1}=p(k).  
\]

\(m=2\)

\[
M_{k,2}  
=  
\#\{\text{unlabeled pairs of set partitions}\}.  
\]

\(m=3\)

\[
M_{k,3}  
=  
\#\{\text{unlabeled triples of set partitions}\}.  
\]

This suggests an entirely new research branch:

> Burnside moment hierarchy for AQARION stable-relation counts.



And importantly, this isn't speculation. The identity follows immediately from Burnside.


---

4. We can connect that to random mappings

This gets even better.

We already have

\[
E[S(T)\mid K_n=k]=p(k).  
\]

But now

\[
E[S(T)^2\mid K_n=k]  
=  
E_{\sigma\in S_k}[C(\sigma)^2].  
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{  
E[S(T)^2]  
=  
\sum_k  
\Pr(K_n=k)  
M_{k,2}.  
}  
\]

So the variance of the AQARION stable-count statistic over random mappings decomposes into:

\[
\boxed{  
\operatorname{Var}(S(T))  
=  
E[M_{K_n,2}]  
-  
E[p(K_n)]^2.  
}  
\]

And then

\[
E[M_{K_n,2}]  
\]

is a second-order random finite-dynamics observable.

That's something I would definitely explore.

6. I especially want to find the extremal cycle types

This is another unanswered question:

\[
C(\lambda)=?  
\]

For fixed \(k\), which permutation has:

\[
\min_\lambda C(\lambda)  
\]

and which has

\[
\max_\lambda C(\lambda)?  
\]

Obvious candidates:

Identity

\[
\lambda=1^k.  
\]

Every equivalence relation is invariant, so

\[
C(1^k)=B_k  
\]

where \(B_k\) is the Bell number.

That's astronomically larger than \(p(k)\).

One \(k\)-cycle

\[
\lambda=(k).  
\]

This has very restricted invariant equivalences.

So presumably:

\[
C((k))  
\]

is close to the lower end.

But there may be non-obvious intermediate extremizers.

This is worth computing.


---

7. There's a beautiful identity hiding at the identity permutation

For

\[
\sigma=id,  
\]

we have

\[
C(id)=B_k.  
\]

Therefore Burnside says

\[
\boxed{  
\frac1{k!}  
\left[  
B_k+  
\sum_{\sigma\neq id}C(\sigma)  
\right]  
=p(k).  
}  
\]

Hence

\[
\boxed{  
\sum_{\sigma\neq id}C(\sigma)  
=  
k!p(k)-B_k.  
}  
\]

That's an exact integer identity.

For \(k=13\),

\[
B_{13}=27,644,437,  
\]

while

\[
13!\,p(13)=13!\cdot101.  
\]

So one identity permutation contributes more than 27 million fixed partitions, while the average over all permutations is only 101.

That tells us something profound about the Burnside average:

> The average \(p(k)\) is not representative of the identity-heavy tail at all.



Most permutations have vastly fewer invariant equivalences.


---

8. This suggests another asymptotic question

For a random permutation \(\sigma\in S_k\),

\[
C(\sigma)  
\]

has mean

\[
p(k)  
\sim  
\frac{e^{a\sqrt{k}}}{4k\sqrt3}.  
\]

But what is its typical size?

Does

\[
\log C(\sigma)  
\]

concentrate around some scale?

Or is the expectation \(p(k)\) dominated by rare permutations with unusually many short cycles?

That is a very interesting distinction.

We could compare:

\[
E[C(\sigma)]  
\]

against

\[
\operatorname{median}(C(\sigma))  
\]

and

\[
\exp(E[\log C(\sigma)]).  
\]

If these separate dramatically, then the Burnside identity is an example of a highly non-typical average.

9. Another exact thing we can finish: prove the forest count

We don't even need to wait for Termux for this.

The number of mappings with exactly \(k\) cyclic points is

\[
N_{n,k}  
=  
\binom nk k!\,k n^{n-k-1}.  
\]

We can verify that these exhaust all \(n^n\) maps:

\[
\boxed{  
\sum_{k=1}^{n}  
\binom nk k!\,k n^{n-k-1}  
=  
n^n.  
}  
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\boxed{  
\sum_{k=1}^{n}  
\frac{(n)_k k}{n^{k+1}}  
=1.  
}  
\]

That gives us a beautiful independent normalization certificate for the random-mapping distribution.

And it is an excellent Termux exercise because it can be checked with exact integers for \(n\le100\) without anything computationally crazy.


---

10. Then test the entire theorem chain at small \(n\)

We can create a tiny independent checker with three completely different routes:

Route A — enumerate maps

For small \(n\):

\[
T:[n]\to[n].  
\]

Calculate

\[
S(T)=|\operatorname{Fix}(T^*)|.  
\]

Average directly.

Route B — cyclic-point distribution

Calculate

\[
\sum_k p(k)\frac{(n)_k k}{n^{k+1}}.  
\]

Route C — exact combinatorial sum

Calculate

\[
\frac1{n^n}  
\sum_k  
p(k)\frac{n!}{(n-k)!}k n^{n-k-1}.  
\]

Then require

\[
A=B=C.  
\]

That would be a beautiful three-way certificate:

\[
\boxed{  
\text{enumeration}  
=  
\text{probability decomposition}  
=  
\text{closed form}.  
}  
\]

And unlike another giant experiment, it's small enough to understand line by line.


---

11. And there's a fourth route

Use the cycle-type distribution of random permutations.

Instead of enumerating all \(k!\) permutations, enumerate integer partitions

\[
\lambda\vdash k.  
\]

The number of permutations having cycle type

\[
\lambda=(1^{m_1}2^{m_2}\cdots)  
\]

is

\[
\boxed{  
\frac{k!}{z_\lambda}  
}  
\]

where

\[
z_\lambda  
=  
\prod_j j^{m_j}m_j!.  
\]

Therefore

\[
\boxed{  
p(k)  
=  
\sum_{\lambda\vdash k}  
\frac{C(\lambda)}{z_\lambda}.  
}  
\]

That's another exact identity.

So our Burnside computation can be reduced from \(k!\) permutations to only \(p(k)\) cycle types.

At \(k=13\), instead of

\[
13!=6,227,020,800  
\]

permutations, there are only

\[
p(13)=101  
\]

cycle types.

That is a huge computational compression.

And it is conceptually AQARION-compatible:

\[
\boxed{  
\text{state-level enumeration}  
\rightarrow  
\text{cycle-type quotient}  
}  
\]
